claim: The mouse tendon cell fate requires continuous maintenance in vivo.
source: In this study, we find that the mouse tendon cell fate requires continuous maintenance in vivo and identify an essential role for TGFβ signaling in maintenance of the tendon cell fate.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and introduction, supported by experimental data showing tenocyte dedifferentiation in mutants.

claim: TGFβ signaling plays an essential role in maintenance of the tendon cell fate.
source: In this study, we find that the mouse tendon cell fate requires continuous maintenance in vivo and identify an essential role for TGFβ signaling in maintenance of the tendon cell fate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that loss of Tgfbr2 leads to tenocyte dedifferentiation and viral reintroduction rescues the phenotype.

claim: Tendon development was not disrupted in Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutant embryos.
source: Tendon development was not disrupted in mutant embryos, but shortly after birth tenocytes lost differentiation markers and reverted to a more stem/progenitor state.
evidence: Supported by data showing normal tendon formation at E14.5 and expression of tendon markers during embryonic development.

claim: Shortly after birth, tenocytes in Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutants lost differentiation markers.
source: Tendon development was not disrupted in mutant embryos, but shortly after birth tenocytes lost differentiation markers and reverted to a more stem/progenitor state.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and in situ hybridization data showing loss of ScxGFP, tenomodulin, and Col1a1 expression in postnatal stages.

claim: Tenocytes in Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutants reverted to a more stem/progenitor state.
source: Tendon development was not disrupted in mutant embryos, but shortly after birth tenocytes lost differentiation markers and reverted to a more stem/progenitor state.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased colony-forming capacity and expression of stem/progenitor markers Sca-1, CD44, and CD34.

claim: Viral reintroduction of Tgfbr2 to mutants prevented tenocyte dedifferentiation.
source: Viral reintroduction of Tgfbr2 to mutants prevented and even rescued tenocyte dedifferentiation suggesting a continuous and cell autonomous role for TGFβ signaling in cell fate maintenance.
evidence: Supported by AAV-mediated gene delivery experiments showing retention of tendon markers in infected cells.

claim: Viral reintroduction of Tgfbr2 to mutants rescued tenocyte dedifferentiation.
source: Viral reintroduction of Tgfbr2 to mutants prevented and even rescued tenocyte dedifferentiation suggesting a continuous and cell autonomous role for TGFβ signaling in cell fate maintenance.
evidence: Supported by AAV-mediated gene delivery experiments at P1 showing re-expression of tendon markers in infected cells.

claim: TGFβ signaling has a continuous and cell autonomous role in cell fate maintenance.
source: Viral reintroduction of Tgfbr2 to mutants prevented and even rescued tenocyte dedifferentiation suggesting a continuous and cell autonomous role for TGFβ signaling in cell fate maintenance.
evidence: Supported by viral rescue experiments showing that individual cells expressing Tgfbr2 retain tendon markers even when surrounded by mutant cells.

claim: Scleraxis (Scx) is a bHLH transcription factor expressed in tendon cells from progenitor stages and through development.
source: A limited number of transcription factors were so far identified as key regulators of the tendon cell fate including most notably, Scleraxis (Scx), a bHLH transcription factor expressed in tendon cells from progenitor stages and through development (Schweitzer et al., 2001) and Mohawk (Mkx), an atypical homeobox protein with essential roles in the development of the collagen matrix in tendons (Ito et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schweitzer et al., 2001.

claim: Mohawk (Mkx) is an atypical homeobox protein with essential roles in the development of the collagen matrix in tendons.
source: A limited number of transcription factors were so far identified as key regulators of the tendon cell fate including most notably, Scleraxis (Scx), a bHLH transcription factor expressed in tendon cells from progenitor stages and through development (Schweitzer et al., 2001) and Mohawk (Mkx), an atypical homeobox protein with essential roles in the development of the collagen matrix in tendons (Ito et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ito et al., 2010.

claim: Tenomodulin (Tnmd) is a prototypic marker for the tendon cell fate.
source: Prototypic markers for the tendon cell fate also include the transmembrane protein tenomodulin (Tnmd) and collagen type I (Kannus, 2000; Huang et al., 2015), the major building blocks of the tendon fibrillar extracellular matrix that mediates the transmission of force by tendons.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kannus, 2000 and Huang et al., 2015.

claim: Collagen type I is a prototypic marker for the tendon cell fate.
source: Prototypic markers for the tendon cell fate also include the transmembrane protein tenomodulin (Tnmd) and collagen type I (Kannus, 2000; Huang et al., 2015), the major building blocks of the tendon fibrillar extracellular matrix that mediates the transmission of force by tendons.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kannus, 2000 and Huang et al., 2015.

claim: Collagen type I is a major building block of the tendon fibrillar extracellular matrix that mediates the transmission of force by tendons.
source: Prototypic markers for the tendon cell fate also include the transmembrane protein tenomodulin (Tnmd) and collagen type I (Kannus, 2000; Huang et al., 2015), the major building blocks of the tendon fibrillar extracellular matrix that mediates the transmission of force by tendons.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kannus, 2000 and Huang et al., 2015, and general knowledge of tendon biology.

claim: TGFβ signaling plays a central role in early events of tendon development.
source: Previous studies have also established a central role for the transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) signaling pathway in early events of tendon development (Pryce et al., 2009; Havis et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pryce et al., 2009 and Havis et al., 2016.

claim: TGFβ is a potent inducer of Scx both in vivo and in cultured cells.
source: Notably, TGFβ is a potent inducer of Scx both in vivo and in cultured cells and disruption of TGFβ signaling in mouse limb bud mesenchyme resulted in complete failure of tendon formation (Pryce et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pryce et al., 2009.

claim: Disruption of TGFβ signaling in mouse limb bud mesenchyme resulted in complete failure of tendon formation.
source: Notably, TGFβ is a potent inducer of Scx both in vivo and in cultured cells and disruption of TGFβ signaling in mouse limb bud mesenchyme resulted in complete failure of tendon formation (Pryce et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pryce et al., 2009.

claim: Subcutaneous application of growth and differentiation factors (GDFs) can induce ectopic neo-tendon formation in rats.
source: Moreover, subcutaneous application of growth and differentiation factors (GDFs), members of the TGFβ superfamily, can induce ectopic neo-tendon formation in rats (Wolfman et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolfman et al., 1997.

claim: TGFβ ligands act by binding to transmembrane type II receptors, which in turn recruit and activate a type I receptor.
source: These ligands act by binding to transmembrane type II receptors, which in turn recruit and activate a type I receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TGFβ signaling mechanism.

claim: The activated TGFβ receptor complex phosphorylates and activates Smad2/3 transcription factors.
source: The activated receptor complex subsequently phosphorylates and activates receptor-regulated transcription factors called Smads (Smad2/3 for TGFβ signaling) that then complex with the common-mediator Smad4 and translocate into the nucleus where they promote or repress responsive target genes (Vander Ark et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vander Ark et al., 2018 and established knowledge of TGFβ signaling.

claim: TGFβ proper ligands (TGFβ1–3) all bind to a single type II receptor.
source: The TGFβ proper ligands (TGFβ1–3) all bind to a single type II receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TGFβ receptor specificity.

claim: Disrupting the TGFβ type II receptor is sufficient to abrogate all TGFβ signaling.
source: Consequently, disrupting this one receptor is sufficient to abrogate all TGFβ signaling.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the fact that all TGFβ ligands bind to the same type II receptor.

claim: ScxCre activity in tenocytes is not uniform during embryogenesis.
source: ScxCre activity in tenocytes is not uniform during embryogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and complete targeting of tenocytes is achieved only in early postnatal stages.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Complete targeting of tenocytes by ScxCre is achieved only in early postnatal stages.
source: ScxCre activity in tenocytes is not uniform during embryogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and complete targeting of tenocytes is achieved only in early postnatal stages.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing nearly complete loss of receptor expression by P0.

claim: By P0, mutant tendons displayed a nearly complete loss of TGFβ type II receptor expression.
source: Indeed, immunostaining for TGFβ type II receptor revealed that by P0 mutant tendons displayed a nearly complete loss of receptor expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutant embryos developed a complete network of tendons by E14.5.
source: Consequently, Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutant embryos developed a complete network of tendons by E14.5, indicating they have bypassed the early requirement for TGFβ signaling in tendon development (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by whole-mount imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mutant pups appeared normal at birth.
source: Mutant tendon development was not perturbed through embryogenesis and mutant pups appeared normal at birth (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: By day 3 after birth (P3), mutant pups showed physical abnormalities including abducted paws and splayed limbs.
source: However, by day 3 after birth (P3), mutant pups showed physical abnormalities that manifested in abducted paws, splayed limbs (Figure 1C, black arrowhead) and severe movement limitations.
evidence: Supported by images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mutant pups showed severe movement limitations by P3.
source: However, by day 3 after birth (P3), mutant pups showed physical abnormalities that manifested in abducted paws, splayed limbs (Figure 1C, black arrowhead) and severe movement limitations.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: A few lateral limb tendons in mutants underwent fragmentation and disintegrated.
source: A few lateral limb tendons, for example the extensor carpi radialis longus tendon underwent fragmentation and disintegrated (Figure 1B, yellow arrowhead and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), whereas the majority of other tendons, notably the extensor digitorium communis tendons, retained structural integrity with a substantial loss of ScxGFP signal (Figure 1B, white arrowhead).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The majority of tendons in mutants retained structural integrity with a substantial loss of ScxGFP signal.
source: A few lateral limb tendons, for example the extensor carpi radialis longus tendon underwent fragmentation and disintegrated (Figure 1B, yellow arrowhead and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), whereas the majority of other tendons, notably the extensor digitorium communis tendons, retained structural integrity with a substantial loss of ScxGFP signal (Figure 1B, white arrowhead).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Substantial loss of ScxGFP was detected in all tendons and related tissues including hindlimb and tail tendons, ligaments and the annulus fibrosus of the intervertebral disc.
source: Substantial loss of ScxGFP was also detected in all tendons and related tissues, including hindlimb and tail tendons, ligaments and the annulus fibrosus of the intervertebral disc (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Loss of ScxGFP signal was gradual starting around P2-P3.
source: Loss of ScxGFP signal was gradual starting around P2-P3, that is before the manifestation of physical abnormalities (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by time-course imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All mutant tendon cells lost ScxGFP at P7.
source: All mutant tendon cells lost ScxGFP at P7.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All mutants died at or before P14.
source: Regardless, all mutants died at or before P14 likely due to ScxCre activity in developing cardiac valves (Levay et al., 2008), leading to enlarged heart as evidenced by gross examination and histological analysis (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the study, with speculation about the cause based on citation to Levay et al., 2008.

claim: The flexor carpi radialis tendons of mutant embryos were consistently torn by E16.5.
source: The flexor carpi radialis tendons of mutant embryos were consistently torn by E16.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Expression of the prototypic tenocyte markers Scx, tenomodulin and collagen I was not disrupted in any tendon of mutant embryos.
source: Moreover, expression of the prototypic tenocyte markers Scx, tenomodulin and collagen I (Figure 2A–D) and the development of the collagen matrix were not disrupted in any tendon of mutant embryos (Figure 2E,F), including the flexor carpi radialis tendon before it snapped.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence, in situ hybridization, and TEM data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The development of the collagen matrix was not disrupted in any tendon of mutant embryos.
source: Moreover, expression of the prototypic tenocyte markers Scx, tenomodulin and collagen I (Figure 2A–D) and the development of the collagen matrix were not disrupted in any tendon of mutant embryos (Figure 2E,F), including the flexor carpi radialis tendon before it snapped.
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Despite functional defects starting around P3, collagen matrix organization in mutant neonates was indistinguishable from that of their wild-type littermates.
source: Surprisingly, despite the functional defects and loss of ScxGFP signal starting around P3, collagen fibers in mutant tendons appeared organized and indistinguishable from those of wild-type (WT) littermates at this stage (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Apparent collagen degradation was observed only in older mutant pups (≥P7).
source: Apparent collagen degradation was observed only in older mutant pups (≥P7) (Figure 3C–G), suggesting the disruption to the matrix of these tendons may be a secondary consequence of the cellular changes in these mutants and/or of their movement difficulties.
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3C–G.

claim: Disruption to the matrix of mutant tendons may be a secondary consequence of the cellular changes in these mutants and/or of their movement difficulties.
source: Apparent collagen degradation was observed only in older mutant pups (≥P7) (Figure 3C–G), suggesting the disruption to the matrix of these tendons may be a secondary consequence of the cellular changes in these mutants and/or of their movement difficulties.
evidence: This is speculation based on the temporal sequence of events observed in the study.

claim: Epitenon was gradually disrupted in mutant pups.
source: Furthermore, epitenon, a monolayer of cells that engulf and define the boundary of the tendon (Kannus, 2000) (Figure 3F, black arrowhead), was gradually disrupted and in some cases was almost undetectable in older mutant pups (Figure 3G, white arrowhead), suggesting that loss of the tendon boundary is an additional feature of the phenotype in these mutants.
evidence: Supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Loss of the tendon boundary is an additional feature of the phenotype in Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutants.
source: Furthermore, epitenon, a monolayer of cells that engulf and define the boundary of the tendon (Kannus, 2000) (Figure 3F, black arrowhead), was gradually disrupted and in some cases was almost undetectable in older mutant pups (Figure 3G, white arrowhead), suggesting that loss of the tendon boundary is an additional feature of the phenotype in these mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of epitenon disruption.

claim: In P7 WT pups, all tendon cells were positive for ScxGFP, Tnmd and Col1a1.
source: In P7 WT pups, all tendon cells were positive for ScxGFP, Tnmd and Col1a1 (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: Most cells in mutant tendons lost the ScxGFP signal and tendon marker gene expression.
source: Conversely, most cells in mutant tendons lost the ScxGFP signal and tendon marker gene expression (Figure 4B, white arrowhead and Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Some cells in mutant tendons retained ScxGFP signal and appeared rounded and enlarged from P3 onwards.
source: Interestingly, some cells in mutant tendons retained ScxGFP signal and appeared rounded and enlarged from P3 onwards (Figure 4B, yellow arrowhead).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Some ScxGFP-positive cells in mutant tendons are newly recruited tendon cells.
source: Some of these cells exhibited weak or no expression of the Ai14 Rosa26-tdTomato (RosaT) Cre reporter (Madisen et al., 2010), suggesting a recent activation of the Scx enhancer in these cells and therefore that they are newly recruited tendon cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of weak RosaT expression in some ScxGFP-positive cells.

claim: Cell death was not detected in mutant tendons throughout developmental stages from E14.5 to P7.
source: Using TUNEL assay, we did not detect cell death in mutant tendons and the rate of tenocyte proliferation as examined by EdU assay was also not altered in these tendons during different developmental stages ranging from E14.5 to P10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting the cell population of mutant tendons was not altered.
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The rate of tenocyte proliferation was not altered in mutant tendons during developmental stages ranging from E14.5 to P10.
source: Using TUNEL assay, we did not detect cell death in mutant tendons and the rate of tenocyte proliferation as examined by EdU assay was also not altered in these tendons during different developmental stages ranging from E14.5 to P10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting the cell population of mutant tendons was not altered.
evidence: Supported by EdU assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The cell population of mutant tendons was not altered.
source: Using TUNEL assay, we did not detect cell death in mutant tendons and the rate of tenocyte proliferation as examined by EdU assay was also not altered in these tendons during different developmental stages ranging from E14.5 to P10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting the cell population of mutant tendons was not altered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of cell death and unchanged proliferation rate.

claim: All ScxGFP-negative cells within mutant tendons were positive for the RosaT Cre reporter.
source: We found that all ScxGFP-negative cells within mutant tendons were positive for the RosaT Cre reporter (Figure 4D, white arrowhead).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The ScxGFP-negative cells in the mutant tendons were derived from tenocytes.
source: This result thus indicates that the ScxGFP-negative cells in the mutant tendons were derived from tenocytes, and highlighted an unexpected reversibility for the tendon cell fate where it was possible for committed and functional tenocytes to lose their differentiation status.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lineage tracing data showing RosaT positivity in ScxGFP-negative cells.

claim: There is an unexpected reversibility for the tendon cell fate where committed and functional tenocytes can lose their differentiation status.
source: This result thus indicates that the ScxGFP-negative cells in the mutant tendons were derived from tenocytes, and highlighted an unexpected reversibility for the tendon cell fate where it was possible for committed and functional tenocytes to lose their differentiation status.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lineage tracing data and loss of tendon markers.

claim: Targeting of Tgfbr2 using ubiquitous inducible cre drivers did not result in tenocyte dedifferentiation.
source: Interestingly, the cell fate of targeted cells was not disrupted in these mutants as evidenced by retention of tendon marker expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F for Tgfbr2;RosaCreERT2 mutants.

claim: A mere loss of TGFβ signaling is not sufficient to cause tenocyte dedifferentiation.
source: This result suggests that a mere loss of TGFβ signaling is not sufficient to cause tenocyte dedifferentiation, and additional factors associated with the loss of Tgfbr2 in the spatial and temporal features determined by ScxCre activity may also play a critical role in this process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between Tgfbr2;ScxCre and Tgfbr2;RosaCreERT2 mutants.

claim: Additional factors associated with the loss of Tgfbr2 in the spatial and temporal features determined by ScxCre activity may play a critical role in tenocyte dedifferentiation.
source: This result suggests that a mere loss of TGFβ signaling is not sufficient to cause tenocyte dedifferentiation, and additional factors associated with the loss of Tgfbr2 in the spatial and temporal features determined by ScxCre activity may also play a critical role in this process.
evidence: This is speculation based on the differential outcomes between different Cre drivers.

claim: Loss of tendon gene expression in mutant tendon cells was not due to transdifferentiation.
source: Using histological staining for the prototypic markers of osteocytes, adipocytes and chondrocytes, we found that loss of tendon gene expression in the cells of mutant tendons was also not due to transdifferentiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the changes in mutant tendons may reflect a process of cellular dedifferentiation.
evidence: Supported by histological staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The changes in mutant tendons may reflect a process of cellular dedifferentiation.
source: Using histological staining for the prototypic markers of osteocytes, adipocytes and chondrocytes, we found that loss of tendon gene expression in the cells of mutant tendons was also not due to transdifferentiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the changes in mutant tendons may reflect a process of cellular dedifferentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the exclusion of cell death and transdifferentiation as explanations for the phenotype.

claim: About 1–2% of cells isolated from tendons of P7 WT and heterozygous controls formed colonies in culture.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, about 1–2% of cells (ScxGFP-positive and RosaT-positive) isolated from tendons of P7 WT and heterozygous controls formed colonies in culture, similar to the frequency of colony forming cells reported in other studies (Bi et al., 2007; Rui et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by colony-forming assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was a significant eightfold increase in the frequency of colony-forming cells in mutant tendons.
source: On the other hand, we found a significant eightfold increase (p<0.01) in the frequency of colony-forming cells in mutant tendons (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by colony-forming assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mutant tendon cells acquired expression of stem cell antigen-1 (Sca-1) and CD44 in postnatal stages.
source: We next screened the mutant tendons for expression of stem/progenitor cell markers and found that the Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutant tendon cells gradually acquired expression of stem cell antigen-1 (Sca-1) and CD44 in postnatal stages (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of Sca-1 was undetectable in WT tendon cells.
source: Notably, expression of Sca-1 was undetectable and CD44 was detected only in very few WT tendon cells, but surprisingly robust expression of these markers was detected in the epitenon (Figure 5C, white arrowheads), a possible source of progenitor cells (Mendias et al., 2012; Dyment et al., 2013; Mienaltowski et al., 2013; Harvey et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CD44 was detected only in very few WT tendon cells.
source: Notably, expression of Sca-1 was undetectable and CD44 was detected only in very few WT tendon cells, but surprisingly robust expression of these markers was detected in the epitenon (Figure 5C, white arrowheads), a possible source of progenitor cells (Mendias et al., 2012; Dyment et al., 2013; Mienaltowski et al., 2013; Harvey et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Robust expression of Sca-1 and CD44 was detected in the epitenon.
source: Notably, expression of Sca-1 was undetectable and CD44 was detected only in very few WT tendon cells, but surprisingly robust expression of these markers was detected in the epitenon (Figure 5C, white arrowheads), a possible source of progenitor cells (Mendias et al., 2012; Dyment et al., 2013; Mienaltowski et al., 2013; Harvey et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The epitenon is a possible source of progenitor cells.
source: Notably, expression of Sca-1 was undetectable and CD44 was detected only in very few WT tendon cells, but surprisingly robust expression of these markers was detected in the epitenon (Figure 5C, white arrowheads), a possible source of progenitor cells (Mendias et al., 2012; Dyment et al., 2013; Mienaltowski et al., 2013; Harvey et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mendias et al., 2012; Dyment et al., 2013; Mienaltowski et al., 2013; Harvey et al., 2019.

claim: At E14.5, low or no expression of Sca-1 and CD44 was found in differentiating tendon cells.
source: At E14.5, at the onset of tendon cell differentiation, we found low or no expression of both markers in the differentiating tendon cells.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: At E14.5, robust positive staining for Sca-1 and CD44 was detected in the cells that surround the tendon, likely the precursors of the epitenon/paratenon.
source: Robust positive staining for both markers was however detected in the cells that surround the tendon at this stage, likely the precursors of the epitenon/paratenon (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sca-1 and CD44 are not markers for tendon progenitor in vivo.
source: These findings suggest that Sca-1 and CD44 are not markers for tendon progenitor in vivo, and possibly simply reflect a generic stemness state of the dedifferentiated mutant tendon cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of these markers in embryonic tendon progenitors.

claim: Sca-1 and CD44 possibly reflect a generic stemness state of the dedifferentiated mutant tendon cells.
source: These findings suggest that Sca-1 and CD44 are not markers for tendon progenitor in vivo, and possibly simply reflect a generic stemness state of the dedifferentiated mutant tendon cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the expression pattern of these markers.

claim: Mutant tendon cells acquired some generic stem/progenitor properties while losing their cell fate.
source: Taken together, our findings show that mutant tendon cells acquired some generic stem/progenitor properties while losing their cell fate.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the colony-forming assay and stem/progenitor marker expression data.

claim: Absence of TGFβ signaling in dedifferentiated cells might prevent them from acquiring the full spectrum of stemness or plasticity.
source: It should be noted however that although these dedifferentiated tendon cells demonstrate some stem/progenitor properties, absence of TGFβ signaling in these cells might prevent them from acquiring the full spectrum of stemness or plasticity.
evidence: This is speculation about the limitations of the dedifferentiated state.

claim: Two major clusters corresponding to WT tenocytes and mutant (dedifferentiated) tendon cells were identified in scRNASeq analysis.
source: Using unsupervised hierarchical clustering analysis, we identified two major clusters corresponding to WT tenocytes and mutant (dedifferentiated) tendon cells in the respective samples (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The WT tenocyte cluster was defined by the expression of tendon markers including Scx, Fmod, Col11a1, Col1a1 and Tnmd.
source: The WT tenocyte cluster was defined by the expression of tendon markers including Scx, Fmod, Col11a1, Col1a1 and Tnmd.
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data.

claim: The mutant (dedifferentiated) tendon cell cluster is enriched for Ly6a (encoding Sca-1) and expresses undetectable level of tendon markers.
source: The mutant (dedifferentiated) tendon cell cluster is enriched for Ly6a (encoding Sca-1) and expresses undetectable level of tendon markers.
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data.

claim: Expression of 186 genes was significantly different between P7 WT tenocytes and mutant cell clusters.
source: In total, expression of 186 genes was significantly different between the two cell populations (≥2 fold change and adjusted p-value<0.05), in which expression of 89 genes was upregulated and 97 genes was downregulated in the mutant tendon cells (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data analysis.

claim: Almost 30% of the downregulated genes (29 genes) were identified as tendon distinctive genes.
source: Almost 30% of the downregulated genes (29 genes) were identified in transcriptome analyses as tendon distinctive genes [(Havis et al., 2014) and our unpublished data].
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data analysis and citation to Havis et al., 2014.

claim: Scx, Fmod, Tnmd, Pdgfrl, Col1a1, Col1a2, Col11a1 and Col11a2 were among the top 25 down-regulated genes in Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutant tendon cells.
source: Notably, the genes Scx, Fmod, Tnmd, Pdgfrl, Col1a1, Col1a2, Col11a1 and Col11a2 were among the top 25 down-regulated genes in Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutant tendon cells (Table 1), further confirming the loss-of-cell fate phenotype in these cells.
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data shown in Table 1.

claim: Expression of the Ly6a gene (encoding Sca-1) was greatly enriched in P7 mutant cells.
source: On the other hand, expression of the Ly6a gene (encoding Sca-1) was greatly enriched in P7 mutant cells, corroborating the IHC findings presented above (Table 2 and Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data shown in Table 2 and immunofluorescence data in Figure 5B.

claim: There was a significant increase in the expression of the Cd34 gene in P7 mutant cells.
source: Moreover, we also found a significant increase in the expression of the Cd34 gene, another common marker for diverse progenitor cells.
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data shown in Table 2.

claim: CD34 protein was detected in mutant cells but not in normal tendon cells.
source: This observation was further confirmed at protein level, where positive immunostaining for CD34 was detected in mutant cells but not in normal tendon cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Several genes upregulated in mutant cells were previously reported to be enriched during embryonic tendon development.
source: Interestingly, the genes upregulated in the mutant cells included several genes (Dpt, Anxa1, Cd34, Cd44, Mgp and Mfap5) whose expression was previously reported to be enriched during embryonic tendon development (Havis et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data and citation to Havis et al., 2014.

claim: The mutant cells may have induction of some developmental programs, a general feature in cellular dedifferentiation.
source: These findings thus do not only lend support to our notion that the mutant cells lost their differentiation state, but also suggest the possibility of induction of some developmental programs in these cells, a general feature in cellular dedifferentiation (Tata et al., 2013; Stocum, 2017; Nusse et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the upregulation of embryonic genes, supported by citations to Tata et al., 2013; Stocum, 2017; Nusse et al., 2018.

claim: One of the prominent biological changes observed in P7 mutant cells was upregulation of gene sets associated with wound healing.
source: Intriguingly, GO enrichment analysis revealed that one of the prominent biological changes observed in P7 mutant cells was upregulation of gene sets associated with wound healing (Figure 6C and Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Genes upregulated in mutant cells associated with wound healing include protease inhibitors (Serpine2, Serping1), inflammatory mediator Anxa1 and extracellular matrix (Col3a1 and Col5a1).
source: These genes include protease inhibitors (Serpine2, Serping1), inflammatory mediator Anxa1 and extracellular matrix (Col3a1 and Col5a1).
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data and GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Tendon cells may play a role in responses to pathological conditions.
source: This finding suggests a possible role for tendon cells in the responses to pathological conditions, in line with findings reported by others (Dakin et al., 2015; Stolk et al., 2017; Schoenenberger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the upregulation of wound healing genes, supported by citations to Dakin et al., 2015; Stolk et al., 2017; Schoenenberger et al., 2018.

claim: Many biological processes downregulated in P7 mutant cells involved collagen synthesis and organization.
source: On the other hand, many biological processes downregulated in P7 mutant cells involved collagen synthesis and organization (Figure 6D and Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Expression of the activating protein 1 (AP-1) transcriptional complex was significantly induced in mutant cells.
source: Notably, expression of the activating protein 1 (AP-1) transcriptional complex, associated with numerous cellular processes including cell fate regulation (Hess et al., 2004), was significantly induced in mutant cells.
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data showing upregulation of Fos and Junb genes.

claim: Expression of both AP-1 components, Fos and Junb genes, was induced more than twofold in mutant cells.
source: Expression of both AP-1 components, that is the Fos and Junb genes was induced more than twofold, and the Jun gene was induced only slightly less than twofold.
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data.

claim: The Id3 gene encoding for a general bHLH transcription factor inhibitor was induced in mutant cells.
source: Moreover, the Id3 gene encoding for a general bHLH transcription factor inhibitor was also induced.
evidence: Supported by scRNASeq data.

claim: Id3 has been implicated in numerous cellular processes including the regulation of cellular differentiation.
source: Due to its broad selection of targets, Id3 was also implicated in numerous cellular processes including the regulation of cellular differentiation (Norton, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Norton, 2000.

claim: Targeted expression of TGFβ type II receptor in E16.5 mutant tendon cells using AAV1-FLEX-Tgfbr2-V5 prevented the loss of tendon markers in the infected tenocytes.
source: Interestingly, targeted re-expression of Tgfbr2-V5 in individual mutant tendon cell at both developmental stages was able to prevent the loss of tendon markers as observed in postnatal pups (Figure 7B–D), suggesting a cell autonomous role for TGFβ signaling in maintenance of the tendon cell fate.
evidence: Supported by AAV infection and immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B–D.

claim: About 95–98% of the AAV-infected (V5-positive) mutant tendon cells retained or re-expressed tendon differentiation markers after viral injection at different developmental stages.
source: Quantification shows that about 95–98% of the AAV-infected (V5-positive) mutant tendon cells retained or re-expressed tendon differentiation markers after viral injection at different developmental stages (n = 3 pups for each stage).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Reactivation of TGFβ signaling in a dedifferentiating tenocyte can reverse the process and rescue a tenocyte from dedifferentiation.
source: Recognizing that cell autonomous activity of Tgfbr2-V5 was sufficient to prevent dedifferentiation of mutant tenocytes, we next wanted to test if reactivation of TGFβ signaling in a dedifferentiating tenocyte could also reverse the process and rescue a tenocyte from dedifferentiation.
evidence: This is a research question addressed by the P1 AAV infection experiment.

claim: All infected mutant tendon cells expressed the tendon markers ScxGFP and tenomodulin after P1 injection with AAV1-Tgfbr2-FLAG.
source: We found again that all infected mutant tendon cells expressed the tendon markers ScxGFP and tenomodulin (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that reactivation of TGFβ signaling was indeed sufficient to rescue the dedifferentiated tenocytes.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Reactivation of TGFβ signaling was sufficient to rescue the dedifferentiated tenocytes.
source: We found again that all infected mutant tendon cells expressed the tendon markers ScxGFP and tenomodulin (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that reactivation of TGFβ signaling was indeed sufficient to rescue the dedifferentiated tenocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the AAV rescue experiment data.

claim: TGFβ signaling is sufficient to prevent and to rescue the loss-of-tendon cell fate in a cell autonomous manner.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that TGFβ signaling is sufficient to prevent and to rescue the loss-of-tendon cell fate in a cell autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the AAV rescue experiments.

claim: Induction of tendon markers by TGFβ signaling is context-dependent.
source: Notably, induction of tendon gene expression following activation of Tgfbr2-FLAG expression was detected only in dedifferentiated tenocytes and not in cells located outside of tendons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). It was previously shown that TGFβ signaling is a potent inducer of ScxGFP and other tendon markers (Pryce et al., 2009; Maeda et al., 2011; Sakabe et al., 2018). This result however, reflects the fact that induction of tendon markers by TGFβ signaling is context-dependent and further indicates that the tenocytes in mutant pups have dedifferentiated to a state that retained tenogenic potential and the capacity to respond to TGFβ signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that AAV infection induces tendon markers only in dedifferentiated tenocytes, supported by citations to Pryce et al., 2009; Maeda et al., 2011; Sakabe et al., 2018.

claim: The tenocytes in mutant pups have dedifferentiated to a state that retained tenogenic potential and the capacity to respond to TGFβ signaling.
source: This result however, reflects the fact that induction of tendon markers by TGFβ signaling is context-dependent and further indicates that the tenocytes in mutant pups have dedifferentiated to a state that retained tenogenic potential and the capacity to respond to TGFβ signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the AAV rescue experiment showing that dedifferentiated cells can re-express tendon markers upon TGFβ signaling reactivation.

claim: Tenocyte dedifferentiation is directly dependent on the loss of TGFβ signaling.
source: Tenocyte dedifferentiation is directly dependent on the loss of TGFβ signaling since retention or reactivation of the TGFβ receptor in isolated cells prevents or reverses the process of dedifferentiation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the AAV rescue experiments.

claim: Tenocyte dedifferentiation in Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutants may not merely be the result of the loss of intrinsic TGFβ signaling in tendon cells.
source: These observations suggest that tenocyte dedifferentiation in these mutants may not merely be the result of the loss of intrinsic TGFβ signaling in tendon cells, but rather may be caused by an interplay between intrinsic loss of TGFβ signaling and additional external factors associated with the loss of Tgfbr2 with the specific spatial and temporal features of the ScxCre driver.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between Tgfbr2;ScxCre and Tgfbr2;RosaCreERT2 mutants.

claim: Tenocyte dedifferentiation may be caused by an interplay between intrinsic loss of TGFβ signaling and additional external factors associated with the loss of Tgfbr2 with the specific spatial and temporal features of the ScxCre driver.
source: These observations suggest that tenocyte dedifferentiation in these mutants may not merely be the result of the loss of intrinsic TGFβ signaling in tendon cells, but rather may be caused by an interplay between intrinsic loss of TGFβ signaling and additional external factors associated with the loss of Tgfbr2 with the specific spatial and temporal features of the ScxCre driver.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of tenocyte dedifferentiation.

claim: Additional external factors may involve cell-matrix interactions affected by the microenvironment of the mutant tendons or changes in cell-cell contacts in the mutant environment.
source: These additional factors may involve cell-matrix interactions affected by the microenvironment of the mutant tendons or changes in cell-cell contacts in the mutant environment.
evidence: This is speculation about the nature of the additional factors.

claim: Mechanical loading experienced by the pups after birth may play a role in the initiation of cellular dedifferentiation.
source: The fact that the phenotype manifested in early post-natal stages may also suggest that mechanical loading experienced by the pups after birth may play a role in the initiation of cellular dedifferentiation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the timing of phenotype manifestation.

claim: The close relationship between tendon function and mechanical stimulus has been underlined in several studies.
source: The close relationship between tendon function and mechanical stimulus has been underlined in several studies (Nabeshima et al., 1996; Heinemeier and Kjaer, 2011; Galloway et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nabeshima et al., 1996; Heinemeier and Kjaer, 2011; Galloway et al., 2013.

claim: Enhanced mechanical loading may compound with altered features in the structure of the mutant tendons to trigger the initiation of the mutant phenotype.
source: Enhanced mechanical loading may compound with altered features in the structure of the mutant tendons to trigger the initiation of the mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of mechanical loading.

claim: The tendon phenotype of Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutants highlights a likely role for tenocyte dedifferentiation in regenerative processes in tendons and possibly also in the progression of tendon pathology.
source: The tendon phenotype of Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutants highlights a likely role for tenocyte dedifferentiation in regenerative processes in tendons and possibly also in the progression of tendon pathology.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Uncovering the molecular pathways involved in tenocyte dedifferentiation may be important for new strategies for treatments of tendon pathologies.
source: Uncovering the molecular pathways involved in this process may therefore be important for new strategies for treatments of tendon pathologies.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential applications of the research.

claim: The Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutants provide a unique opportunity to analyze the molecular pathways involved in tenocyte dedifferentiation.
source: The Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutants provide a unique opportunity to analyze these pathways, and the experimental approaches employed in this study may be developed into an experimental paradigm for molecular dissection of this process.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the model system.

claim: The dramatic cell fate changes in Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutant happen in the context of a genetic modification.
source: Nevertheless, it is important to recognize that the dramatic cell fate changes in Tgfbr2;ScxCre mutant happens in the context of a genetic modification.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the experimental context.

claim: The occurrence of tenocyte dedifferentiation in vivo might not be a simple direct outcome of changes to TGFβ signaling.
source: The occurrence of such phenomenon in vivo might not be a simple direct outcome of changes to TGFβ signaling.
evidence: This is speculation about the complexity of the in vivo process.

claim: The molecular events that drive the dedifferentiation process downstream of the initiation event are likely similar or related across different scenarios.
source: Most importantly, while the initiating events for tenocyte dedifferentiation may vary in different scenarios, it is likely that the molecular events that drive the dedifferentiation process downstream of the initiation event are similar or related.
evidence: This is speculation about the generalizability of the molecular mechanisms.

claim: Uncovering the molecular pathways of dedifferentiation in this experimental system may facilitate the analysis of such processes in various other contexts.
source: Uncovering these pathways in this experimental system may therefore facilitate the analysis of such processes in various other contexts.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader applicability of the findings.

claim: Tendons are connective tissues that transmit forces from muscle to bone to generate movement.
source: Tendons are connective tissues that transmit forces from muscle to bone to generate movement (Kannus, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kannus, 2000 and general knowledge of tendon function.

claim: Tendons have slow and limited healing capabilities.
source: Despite their importance to overall musculoskeletal function and their slow and limited healing capabilities, relatively little is known about tendon development, the tendon cell fate, maturation and pathology.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tendon biology.

claim: Relatively little is known about tendon development, the tendon cell fate, maturation and pathology.
source: Despite their importance to overall musculoskeletal function and their slow and limited healing capabilities, relatively little is known about tendon development, the tendon cell fate, maturation and pathology.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Dedifferentiation has mostly been studied in vitro.
source: Dedifferentiation has mostly been studied in vitro (Weinberg et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2010; Pennock et al., 2015; Mueller et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2017; Nordmann et al., 2017) and there are only a handful of reported cases of dedifferentiation in vivo (Talchai et al., 2012; Tata et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: There are only a handful of reported cases of dedifferentiation in vivo.
source: Dedifferentiation has mostly been studied in vitro (Weinberg et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2010; Pennock et al., 2015; Mueller et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2017; Nordmann et al., 2017) and there are only a handful of reported cases of dedifferentiation in vivo (Talchai et al., 2012; Tata et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Talchai et al., 2012; Tata et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Cellular dedifferentiation manifests in most cases by loss of features associated with the differentiated state and reversion to an earlier progenitor state within their cell lineage.
source: Cellular dedifferentiation manifests in most cases by loss of features associated with the differentiated state and reversion to an earlier progenitor state within their cell lineage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular dedifferentiation.

claim: Sca-1, CD34 and CD44 are prototypic somatic stem/progenitor markers.
source: Moreover, the mutant tenocytes gained expression of the prototypic somatic stem/progenitor markers Sca-1, CD34 and CD44 (Holmes and Stanford, 2007; Sung et al., 2008; Hittinger et al., 2013; Sidney et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Holmes and Stanford, 2007; Sung et al., 2008; Hittinger et al., 2013; Sidney et al., 2014.

claim: Sca-1 and CD44 are expressed at high levels in cultured tendon-derived stem/progenitor cells.
source: Notably, of these stem/progenitor markers only Sca-1 and CD44 are also expressed at high levels in cultured tendon-derived stem/progenitor cells (Bi et al., 2007; Mienaltowski et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bi et al., 2007; Mienaltowski et al., 2013.

claim: Limb regeneration in amphibians involves dedifferentiation of cells near the wound to blastema.
source: One of the well-studied examples is limb regeneration in amphibians. Following limb amputation, cells near to the wound dedifferentiate to blastema, proliferate and eventually re-differentiate to replace all the components of the lost limb (McCusker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to McCusker et al., 2015.

claim: Following partial heart amputation in zebrafish, sarcomeres in mature cardiomyocytes disassembled, lost their differentiation gene expression profile and switched to embryonic hyperplastic growth.
source: In zebrafish, it has also been reported that following partial heart amputation, sarcomeres in mature cardiomyocytes disassembled, lost their differentiation gene expression profile and switched to embryonic hyperplastic growth to replace the missing tissues (Poss et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Poss et al., 2002.

claim: Cellular dedifferentiation has been observed in murine mature hepatocytes, pancreatic β cells and skeletal muscle cells.
source: Cellular dedifferentiation has also been observed in murine mature hepatocytes (Gournay et al., 2002), pancreatic β cells (Talchai et al., 2012) and skeletal muscle cells (Mu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gournay et al., 2002; Talchai et al., 2012; Mu et al., 2011.

claim: Disruption of the mouse intestinal barrier led to reversion of crypt (epithelial) cells to a fetal-like stem cell state.
source: More recently, Nusse and colleagues (Nusse et al., 2018) have shown that disruption of the mouse intestinal barrier, via either parasitic infection or cell death, led to reversion of crypt (epithelial) cells to a fetal-like stem cell state.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nusse et al., 2018.

claim: Expression of Sca-1 was highly induced in fetal-like intestinal stem cells.
source: Interestingly, expression of Sca-1 was highly induced in these cells, and when cultured the Sca-1 positive crypt cells exhibited characteristics of fetal intestinal epithelium including re-expression of fetal signature genes and loss of differentiated markers.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nusse et al., 2018.

claim: Dedifferentiation may be a generalized cellular response to tissue damage.
source: Taken together, this growing body of evidence suggests that dedifferentiation may be a generalized cellular response to tissue damage that warrants further investigation.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple examples of dedifferentiation in response to injury.

claim: Induction of Sca-1 may serve as a marker for a pathology-related dedifferentiation process.
source: Moreover, these observations may also suggest that induction of Sca-1 may serve as a marker for a pathology-related dedifferentiation process.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of Sca-1 induction in multiple dedifferentiation contexts.

claim: Sca-1-positive cells were found in the wound window in rat patellar tendon incisional injury model.
source: Intriguingly, Sca-1-positive cells were also found in the wound window in rat patellar tendon incisional injury model, but in this case it was not determined if Sca-1 expression was associated with dedifferentiation (Tan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tan et al., 2013.

claim: Sca-1 expression has been identified on putative stem/progenitor cell populations in various tissues.
source: Sca-1 expression has been identified on putative stem/progenitor cell populations in various tissues (Holmes and Stanford, 2007; Hittinger et al., 2013), but little is known about its biological function.
evidence: Supported by citations to Holmes and Stanford, 2007; Hittinger et al., 2013.

claim: Little is known about the biological function of Sca-1.
source: Sca-1 expression has been identified on putative stem/progenitor cell populations in various tissues (Holmes and Stanford, 2007; Hittinger et al., 2013), but little is known about its biological function.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge regarding Sca-1.

claim: TGFβ signaling may have a continuous role in protecting the differentiated tenocytes from dedifferentiation.
source: This result suggests that TGFβ signaling may have a continuous role in protecting the differentiated tenocytes from dedifferentiation, identifying TGFβ signaling as a key regulator of tendon homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments.

claim: TGFβ signaling is a key regulator of tendon homeostasis.
source: This result suggests that TGFβ signaling may have a continuous role in protecting the differentiated tenocytes from dedifferentiation, identifying TGFβ signaling as a key regulator of tendon homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: TGFβ signaling has been implicated in cell fate maintenance in various tissues.
source: Previous studies have implicated TGFβ signaling in cell fate maintenance in various tissues, for example preserving chondrocyte identity in cultures (Baugé et al., 2013) and suppressing intestinal cell dedifferentiation (Cammareri et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baugé et al., 2013 and Cammareri et al., 2017.

claim: This is the first report of TGFβ signaling's role in maintenance of the tendon cell fate.
source: While TGFβ signaling has been associated with different aspects of tendon biology (Pryce et al., 2009; Havis et al., 2016), to the best of our knowledge this is the first report of its role in maintenance of the tendon cell fate.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings.
